q: Douro contracts and lodge records still count in a cask of roughly five hundred and fifty litres, and a shipper's stock is described in them rather than in litres. Name that cask.
exp: The word covers a family of sizes rather than one exact volume, since the shipping pipe of about 534 litres, the valley pipe of 550 and the larger lodge pipe used for ageing all differ. Production of a declared vintage is still quoted in pipes, which is why the figures in a trade report never look like litres.

q: Two bottles of one house's multi-vintage cuvee carry different edition numbers on the label, and no vintage appears anywhere on either. What does that number identify?
opts: The particular blend, so one release can be told from the next
The cellar in which that lot was aged, which the house treats as part of the wine's identity
How long the wine spent on its lees before it was disgorged
The dosage in grams per litre, printed as a code rather than a figure
exp: A multi-vintage blend is remade every year and is never quite the same wine twice, which the old convention of calling it simply non-vintage concealed. Numbering the releases lets a buyer, a sommelier and a critic all refer to one specific assembly, and some houses print a further code that resolves to the disgorgement date.

q: One Reims house prints on every non-vintage bottle the year in which the blend went down into its cellar, so a buyer can work out how long it lay there before release. Give the French phrase used for that statement.
exp: The blend is assembled from one harvest and its reserves and then bottled for its second fermentation, and the year printed is the year that happened. A bottle laid down in one year and released six later has therefore spent that whole span on its lees, which the label of an ordinary non-vintage leaves a buyer to guess at.

q: Tiny quantities of intensely extracted Right Bank red, made in the 1990s in cellars barely larger than the buildings they were nicknamed after, earned their makers a label they never chose. What were they called?
exp: The name began as a jibe about scale and the wines turned it into a marketing category, with prices following critical scores rather than any classification. The style went out of fashion as taste moved back towards freshness, but the argument it started, about whether a small parcel farmed obsessively can outrank a classified estate, has not gone away.

q: Across the top of a bottle of everyday claret run the words Grand Vin de Bordeaux, printed larger than anything else on the label. What does that phrase promise about the wine?
accept: nothing it has no legal meaning
nothing the phrase has no legal force
it is not defined in law
exp: Grand vin has a real use inside a chateau, where it names the estate's first selection as against its second wine, but printed as a slogan on a regional bottling it carries no requirement of any kind. The statements that do bind on that label are the appellation, the vintage and the bottling line, and none of them is usually the largest thing on it.

q: Merchants who want a case of one Vosne-Romanee domaine's grand crus are obliged to take a spread of its lesser wines in the same shipment. What does that practice achieve for the domaine?
opts: It satisfies a Burgundian rule obliging a producer to offer its whole range to any buyer
The whole range moves, the famous bottles carrying the rest with them
It keeps the grand crus out of the auction rooms, where resale is forbidden by the appellation
It lowers the duty due on the shipment, which is levied on the case rather than on the bottle
exp: A village Vosne-Romanee is a harder sell than a grand cru, and tying the two together means the cellar never has to discount either of them. The buyer's compensation is that the door stays open for the next vintage, which is worth more than the margin lost on the wines they did not especially want.

exp: The crus are bottled only when the year justifies them, so a weak vintage yields one wine where a strong one yields ten. It runs against the usual incentive, since the cru bottlings are the profitable ones, and it is why the cooperative's ordinary Barbaresco in a lesser year is better than its price suggests.

q: Chateauneuf-du-Pape permits a long list of varieties, and one celebrated estate there ignores all but a single grape, growing it on sand well back from the stony plateau. Which variety fills that red?
exp: Chateau Rayas is the estate, and its red carries no Syrah, no Mourvedre and nothing else the decree allows. Sand, the shade of surrounding pine woods and very low yields give a wine so pale and perfumed that it is regularly mistaken for red Burgundy blind, which is much of the reason it is argued about.

q: Between the 1960s and the 1980s the delimited area above Ampuis grew several times over, and the growers who had stayed on the terraces objected to the ground being added. Where was that ground?
opts: The flat plateau behind the top of the slope
The left bank of the river, looking back at the terraces
Alluvial islands and river flats lying at the foot of the terraces
Terraces already replanted to Viognier for white wine
exp: The terraces had been abandoned by the hundred because no machine can work them, and planting the plateau behind was the only cheap way to enlarge the appellation. Fruit up there ripens later and rarely carries the perfume of the slope, which is why the appellation name alone now tells a buyer less than it once did.

q: A summer storm at Ampuis can strip the topsoil off a terrace in an hour, and a grower there reckons on more days a year at masonry than at pruning. What is being repaired?
exp: The terraces are held by walls laid without mortar, and no machine can rebuild one; the labour is the reason so much of the slope went out of production in the middle of the twentieth century. Water that gets in behind a wall pushes it out, so the gaps between the stones are not sloppy work but the whole design.

q: A grower at Chavanay picks Viognier off one terrace and Syrah off the next, and bottles the two separately. Which pair of appellations do the wines carry?
opts: Saint-Peray for the white and Crozes-Hermitage for the red
Chateau-Grillet for the white and Cornas for the red
Condrieu for the white and Saint-Joseph for the red
Condrieu for the white and Cote-Rotie for the red
exp: Condrieu and Saint-Joseph overlap across several communes at the northern end of the valley, so a single hillside carries one name or the other according to what is planted on it. Cote-Rotie stops well short of Chavanay to the north, and Chateau-Grillet is a single enclosed amphitheatre a few kilometres upstream of it, at Verin and Saint-Michel-sur-Rhone, that no other grower may use.

q: A sweet Condrieu appears on a list and a guest objects that the appellation covers dry white only. What is the position?
opts: The sweet wine exists but must go out as Chateau-Grillet
The appellation is dry only, so the bottle must be labelled Vin de France
Sweetness is allowed only in a vintage the syndicat declares for it
The decree permits a sweet wine from late-picked fruit, and a little is made most years
exp: Condrieu was historically as often sweet as dry and the decree still allows it, but the wines are rare because Viognier's acidity has usually collapsed by the time the sugar is high enough to be worth leaving. Look for moelleux or doux on the label, since the appellation name on its own will not tell you.

q: Seven communes make Condrieu, and they fall in three different departments, one of which shares its name with a wine region three hundred kilometres to the north. Name the three departments.
accept: departments of rhone loire and ardeche
departments of rhone ardeche and loire
departements of rhone loire and ardeche
exp: The town of Condrieu is in the Rhone, five of the seven communes are in the Loire, and Limony sits across in the Ardeche. The Loire here is the department named for the river's upper course through the Massif Central and has nothing to do with the Loire Valley's wines, and Chateau-Grillet, the enclave inside the Condrieu boundary, lies in it too.

q: A dessert wine turns up from the northern valley, made from bunches dried indoors on racks for weeks before a very slow pressing. Only one appellation there may produce it. Which?
opts: Crozes-Hermitage
Saint-Joseph
Hermitage
Cornas
exp: The straw wine is made from Marsanne and Roussanne raisined on mats or in ventilated lofts, then pressed through the winter, and the ferment can run for a year. Almost none of it leaves the region, but the Hermitage decree provides for it and no other decree in the valley does.

q: Almost all the granite of the northern valley lies on the right bank against the edge of the Massif Central, yet the hill behind Tain and the slopes running north from it stand on the left bank and are cut from the same rock. How did that rock get there?
opts: It is a glacial erratic carried down and dropped by ice off the Alps
It is an uplifted spur of the Alps with the same mineralogy
It is a volcanic cone thrown up long after the Massif had formed
The river shifted west and left a block of the Massif on its east bank
exp: The Rhone once ran east of the hill and later cut a new course to the west of it, marooning a granitic spur of the Massif Central on the left bank. That is also why the hill faces due south while its neighbours face east, and why its fruit ripens so much more completely than theirs. The same stranded block carries on north behind Gervans and Serves, which is why the northern half of Crozes-Hermitage sits on granite while its southern half, out on the flat at Les Chassis, sits on glacial gravel.

q: At the very top of the hill above Tain, beside the chapel, lies a climat named for the solitary who is said to have lived up there. Give the name of that parcel.
exp: The hill's name and the parcel's name come from the same hermit. L'Hermite is the highest of the climats, on thin granite under a cap of windblown silt, and its wine is finer-boned than the wine off the bare granite lower down the western end. It is one of the parcel names most often printed under the appellation.
